docs.title: Family Contribution Management System
docs.text: Welcome to the project documentation for the Family Contribution Management System — a platform for digitizing how families manage meetings, contributions, pledges, and payments.

docs.title: What this project does
docs.text:
Note

This system replaces manual record-keeping (notebooks, spreadsheets, WhatsApp chaos) with a single, transparent, auditable source of truth — while preserving traditional family governance roles: Chairman, Secretary, and Treasurer.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Fixed (AGM-style) and voluntary (pledge-based) contribution campaigns
  • M-Pesa mobile money integration and manual payment tracking
  • Support for phoneless members via Guardian/Proxy accounts
  • A permanent, tamper-proof audit trail
  • Meeting management with attendance and minutes

docs.title: Authentication & Authorization in Backend Development
docs.text:
In the world of software development, ensuring the security and privacy of user data is of utmost importance. Two essential concepts that play a vital role in achieving this are authentication and authorization. These mechanisms work hand in hand to verify the identity of users and determine their level of access to specific resources.We will delve into the significance of authentication and authorization in backend development, and explore how they are implemented using examples.

Tip

Authentication and authorization are the twin pillars of REST API security, serving fundamentally different but sequential purposes. Authentication (AuthN) verifies who the client is, while Authorization (AuthZ) determines what that verified identity is allowed to do. Because REST APIs are architecturally stateless, every incoming request must self-authenticate and demonstrate proper permissions independently

docs.title: Authentication:
docs.text:
Verifying User Identity

Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user attempting to access a system or application. It ensures that the user is who they claim to be. Various authentication methods exist, including passwords, tokens, biometrics, and more. Let's take a look at a few examples:

docs.title: Basic Authentication:
docs.text:
• How it works: The client combines the username and password, encodes them in Base64, and sends them inside the Authorization: Basic header.
  • Trade-offs: Base64 is strictly an encoding format, not encryption. If intercepted, it is easily decoded.
  • Best Use Case: Strictly restricted to internal microservices, testing, or development environments wrapped entirely inside HTTPS/TLS.

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
• How it works: The server generates a unique, long random string for the client. The client appends it to an HTTP header (e.g., X-API-KEY) or query parameter with each request.
  • Trade-offs: Unlike modern tokens, API keys are static, typically do not expire automatically, and require a server-side database lookup to verify validity.
  • Best Use Case: Server-to-server communication, read-only public data distribution, and basic usage tracking/rate limiting.

docs.title: JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
docs.text:
• How it works: A stateless, cryptographically signed token containing user information (payload). Upon a valid login, the server issues a JWT. The client stores it locally and passes it inside the Authorization: Bearer header.
  • Trade-offs: Highly scalable because the server decodes and validates the signature without checking a database. However, because they are stateless, revoking a JWT before its expiration date requires secondary strategies (like blocklists or refresh token rotation).
  • Best Use Case: Single-page applications (SPAs), mobile apps, and distributed microservices requiring stateless scalability

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 Framework
docs.text:
• How it works: A sophisticated delegation framework rather than a simple protocol. It allows a third-party application to obtain limited access to a user’s account using access tokens without ever exposing the user's login credentials.
  • Trade-offs: Highly secure, highly flexible, supports token expiration, and permits fine-grained scopes. The primary drawback is its complexity to set up and manage compared to static methods.
  • Best Use Case: Enterprise-grade security, third-party ecosystem integrations (e.g., "Sign in with Google"), and public developer platforms

Example

  1. Username and Password:  This is the most common form of authentication. Users provide a username and password combination to access a system. The backend verifies the credentials against a stored record, and if they match, the user is authenticated.
  2. Token-based Authentication:  Token-based authentication involves issuing a token to a user upon successful login. The token is then sent with subsequent requests to the server to authenticate the user. One popular implementation is JSON Web Tokens (JWT), which stores user information in an encoded format within the token.
  3. Multi-factor Authentication (MFA):  MFA adds an extra layer of security by requiring users to provide multiple forms of authentication. For example, in addition to a password, a user might need to provide a verification code sent to their mobile device.

docs.title: Authorization: Granting Access to Resources
docs.text:
Authorization is the process of determining what resources a user is allowed to access and what actions they can perform. Once a user is authenticated, their authorization level dictates the operations they can carry out within the system. Once a client is successfully authenticated, the API must restrict resource access through structured authorization frameworks: Let's explore some examples:

Example

  1. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Permissions are assigned to specific administrative roles (e.g., Admin, Editor, Viewer). The API checks if the user's role is permitted to execute the matching HTTP method on that route (e.g., only Admin can access DELETE /users/:id).  RBAC assigns roles to users based on their responsibilities within an organization. Each role is granted specific permissions and access rights. For instance, an admin role might have full access to all resources, while a regular user role may have limited access.
  2. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC):  Fine-grained permission management based on variables like context, time of day, location, or resource ownership (e.g., a user can only PUT /articles/:id if article.ownerId === user.id). ABAC defines access control policies based on various attributes such as user attributes, resource attributes, and environmental attributes. It allows for more granular control over access by considering multiple factors. For example, an access policy might grant read access to a specific resource only during business hours.
  3. Permission-Based Authorization:  Tokens are minted with restricted operational permissions (e.g., read:profile, write:orders). Even an admin user's token cannot execute a write operation if the token itself was only granted. In permission-based authorization, users are granted access based on individual permissions. Each user is associated with a set of permissions that explicitly define what actions they can perform. For instance, a user may have permission to create, read, update, or delete specific resources.

docs.title: Best Practices for Implementing Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
1. Use Secure Password Storage: Ensure that user passwords are securely stored using strong hashing algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2, combined with a unique salt for each user. Additionally, consider implementing password policies, such as enforcing minimum complexity requirements.
  2. Use Strong Encryption: Ensure that sensitive data, such as authentication tokens and session information, is transmitted securely over HTTPS. Implementing strong encryption protocols adds an extra layer of protection against eavesdropping and data tampering.
  3. Implement Session Management:  Proper session management is crucial for maintaining user authentication state. Implement mechanisms like session expiration, session invalidation upon logout, and regenerate session IDs after authentication events.

Note

  1. Regularly Update and Patch Dependencies:  Keep your backend dependencies up to date to benefit from the latest security patches and bug fixes. Outdated libraries can contain vulnerabilities that can be exploited by attackers.
  2. Implement Rate Limiting:  Protect your application from brute-force attacks and denial-of-service (DoS) attempts by implementing rate limiting mechanisms. This limits the number of requests a user can make within a specific timeframe.
  3. Apply Principle of Least Privilege:  Grant users the minimum level of access necessary to perform their tasks. Regularly review and audit user permissions to ensure they align with the principle of least privilege.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Authentication and authorization are essential components of backend development forming the bedrock of secure and reliable systems. By implementing these mechanisms effectively, developers can safeguard their applications against unauthorized access and potential data breaches. Whether you're building a web application, API, or any backend system, prioritizing authentication and authorization is paramount to providing a secure user experience. Remember, authentication verifies user identity, while authorization controls access to resources. Implementing appropriate authentication and authorization methods will help you create a robust backend system that upholds data security and user trust.

docs.title: What database design actually is
docs.text:
Database design is the process of deciding what tables exist, what columns each has, and how tables relate to each other which is done before writing a single line of application code. Get it wrong, and every feature built on top of it inherits the mistake; get it right, and features slot in cleanly.

Note

  • BEFORE MOVING TO NORMALIZATION,LETS FIRST DISCUSS ABOUT FOREIGN KEY AND PRIMARY KEY.

docs.title: Difference between Primary Key and Foreign Key
docs.text:
• Keys are one of the most important elements in a relational database to maintain the relationship between the tables and it also helps in uniquely identifying the data from a table. The primary key is a key that helps uniquely identify the tuple of the database.
  • In contrast, the Foreign Key is a key used to determine the relationship between the tables through the primary key of one table that is the primary key of one table acts as a foreign key to another table. Now, let's discuss both of them in some detail.

docs.title: What is Primary Key?
docs.text: • A primary key is used to ensure that data in the specific column is unique. A column cannot have NULL values. It is either an existing table column or a column that is specifically generated by the database according to a defined sequence.

docs.title: What is Foreign Key?
docs.text: • A foreign key is a column or group of columns in a relational database table that provides a link between data in two tables. It is a column (or columns) that references a column (most often the primary key) of another table.

docs.title: Normalization — the core idea
docs.text:
• Normalization is the discipline of structuring tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. The enemy it fights is redundancy — the same piece of information duplicated across multiple rows — because redundancy causes anomalies: update the fact in one place, forget the other, and now your database contradicts itself.

  • Normalization fixes this by splitting data into separate tables, each owning one kind of fact, connected by references — which is exactly what a Foreign Key is.

  • In database design, handles like FK (Foreign Key) and M2M (Many-to-Many) represent the core mechanics used to establish relationships between tables while maintaining data integrity through normalization.

  • Here is a practical breakdown of how these concepts work together to eliminate redundancy and structure your data correctly.

Example

  • The Role of Foreign Keys (FK): A Foreign Key is a column (or group of columns) in one table that links to a Primary Key (PK) in another table. It is the fundamental tool used to enforce referential integrity and build relationships.
  • 1:Many (One-to-Many) Relationships:

This is the most common relational pattern. You implement it by placing the PK of the "One" side as an FK into the "Many" side.

Example

  • Departments and Employees. One department can have many employees, but an employee belongs to only one department.
  • Implementation: Place DepartmentID as an FK inside the Employees table.

docs.title: Relationships in SQL - One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-Many
docs.text: Relationships in SQL define how tables in a relational database are connected and interact through foreign keys, ensuring data integrity and enabling efficient data retrieval by allowing data to be linked across multiple tables.

docs.title: Type of Relationships in SQL
docs.text:
There are different types of relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, and self-referencing.

  1. One-to-One Relationship.

Each record in Table A is associated with one and only one record in Table B, and vice versa.

- Setup: Include a foreign key in one of the tables that references the primary key of the other table.

Example

Tables users and user_profiles, where each user has a single corresponding profile.

  1. One-to-Many Relationship.

Each record in Table A can be associated with multiple records in Table B, but each record in Table B is associated with only one record in Table A.

- Setup: Include a foreign key in the "many" side table (Table B) that references the primary key of the "one" side table (Table A).

Example

  • Tables departments and employees, where each department can have multiple employees, but each employee belongs to one department.
  1. Many-to-Many Relationship

Each record in Table A can be associated with multiple records in Table B, and vice versa.

- Setup: Create an intermediate table (also known as a junction or linking table) that contains foreign keys referencing both related tables.

Example

  • Tables students and courses, where each student can enroll in multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students.
  1. Many-to-One Relationship

Multiple records in table B can be associated with one record in table A.

- Setup: Crate a Foreign key in "Many Table" that references to Primary Key in "One Table".

Example

  • Table Teachers and Courses, many courses can be taught by single teacher.
  1. Self-Referencing Relationship

A table has a foreign key that references its primary key.

- Setup: Include a foreign key column in the same table that references its primary key.

Example

  • A table employees with a column manager_id referencing the same table's employee_id.

docs.title: Handling Many-to-Many (M2M) Relationships
docs.text:
• Relational databases cannot directly map a Many-to-Many relationship between two tables. If you try, you will violate normalization rules by creating duplicate rows or storing messy, comma-separated lists in a single cell.To solve this, you must break the M2M relationship into.
  • 1:Many relationships using a Junction Table (also known as a join, bridge, or associative table). The M2M PatternScenario: Students and Courses. A student can enroll in multiple courses, and a course can have multiple students.Solution: Create a third table, Enrollments.

docs.title: Database Schema Example
docs.text:
• Students Table: StudentID (PK), StudentName
  • Courses Table: CourseID (PK), CourseName
  • Enrollments Table (Junction):
    • StudentID (FK referencing Students)
    • CourseID (FK referencing Courses)

Note

  • The combination of (StudentID, CourseID) typically forms a Composite Primary Key for this table to prevent duplicate enrollments.

docs.title: What are the benefits of database normalization?
docs.text:
The benefits of database normalization include:

  1. Prevention of data anomalies

When larger, more complicated tables are decomposed (or divided) into smaller, simpler tables, altering a database becomes an easier, less error-prone process, and limits changes to the now-smaller tables of related data.

  1. Reduction of unintentional data redundancy

While intentional data redundancy can help improve data quality, security and availability, uninentional data redundancy is the effect of systems inadvertently creating duplicate data, which results in inefficiencies.

  1. Data storage cost savings

Reducing duplicate data through database normalization can lower data storage costs. This is especially important for cloud environments where pricing is often based on the volume of data storage used.

  1. Faster data retrieval

Less data redundancy due to normalization can also lead to faster data queries as lower redundancy often requires less data processing during searches.

docs.title: Normal Forms in DBMS
docs.text: Normal forms are a set of progressive rules (or design checkpoints) for relational schemas that reduce redundancy and prevent data anomalies. Each normal form ( 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF ) is stricter than the previous one: meeting a higher normal form implies the lower ones are satisfied. Think of them as layers of cleanliness for your tables: the deeper you go, the fewer redundancy and integrity problems you’ll have.

docs.title: Benefits of using Normal Forms
docs.text:
• Reduce duplicate data and wasted storage.
  • Prevent insert, update, and delete anomalies.
  • Improve data consistency and integrity.
  • Make the schema easier to maintain and evolve.

Example

  • Let's break down the various normal forms step-by-step to understand the conditions that need to be satisfied at each level:

docs.title: TYPES OF NORMAL FORMS
docs.text:
1. First Normal Form (1NF): Eliminating Duplicate Records

A table is in 1NF if it satisfies the following conditions:

  • All columns contain atomic values (i.e., indivisible values).
  • Each row is unique (i.e., no duplicate rows).
  • Each column has a unique name.
  • The order in which data is stored does not matter.

Example

1NF Violation: If a table has a column "Phone Numbers" that stores multiple phone numbers in a single cell, it violates 1NF. To bring it into 1NF, you need to separate phone numbers into individual rows.

  1. Second Normal Form (2NF): Eliminating Partial Dependency

A relation is in 2NF if it satisfies the conditions of 1NF and additionally, contains no partial dependency exists, meaning every non-prime attribute (non-key attribute) must depend on the entire primary key, not just a part of it.

Example

For a composite key (StudentID, CourseID), if the "StudentName" depends only on "StudentID" and not on the entire key, it violates 2NF. To normalize, move StudentName into a separate table where it depends only on "StudentID"

  1. Third Normal Form (3NF): Eliminating Transitive Dependency

A relation is in 3NF if it satisfies 2NF and additionally, there are no transitive dependencies. In simpler terms, non-prime attributes should not depend on other non-prime attributes.

Example

Consider a table with (StudentID, CourseID, Instructor). If Instructor depends on "CourseID", and "CourseID" depends on "StudentID", then Instructor indirectly depends on "StudentID", which violates 3NF. To resolve this, place Instructor in a separate table linked by "CourseID".

  1. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): The Strongest Form of 3NF

BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF where for every non-trivial functional dependency (X → Y), X must be a superkey (a unique identifier for a record in the table).

Example

If a table has a dependency (StudentID, CourseID) → Instructor, but neither "StudentID" nor "CourseID" is a superkey, then it violates BCNF. To bring it into BCNF, decompose the table so that each determinant is a candidate key.

  1. Fourth Normal Form (4NF): Removing Multi-Valued Dependencies

A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and has no multi-valued dependencies. A multi-valued dependency occurs when one attribute determines another, and both attributes are independent of all other attributes in the table.

Example

Consider a table where (StudentID, Language, Hobby) are attributes. If a student can have multiple hobbies and languages, a multi-valued dependency exists. To resolve this, split the table into separate tables for Languages and Hobbies.

  1. Fifth Normal Form (5NF): Eliminating Join Dependency

5NF is achieved when a table is in 4NF and all join dependencies are removed. This form ensures that every table is fully decomposed into smaller tables that are logically connected without losing information.

Example

If a table contains (StudentID, Course, Instructor) and there is a dependency where all combinations of these columns are needed for a specific relationship, you would split them into smaller tables to remove redundancy.

docs.title: Common Challenges of Over-Normalization
docs.text:
While normalization is a powerful tool for optimizing databases, it's important not to over-normalize your data.

Excessive normalization can lead to:

  • Complex Queries: Too many tables may result in multiple joins, making queries slow and difficult to manage.

  • Performance Overhead: Additional processing required for joins in overly normalized databases may hurt performance, especially in large-scale systems.

In many cases, denormalization (combining tables to reduce the need for complex joins) is used for performance optimization in specific applications, such as reporting systems.

docs.title: When to Use Normalization and Denormalization
docs.text:
Normalization is best suited for transactional systems where data integrity is paramount, such as banking systems and enterprise applications.

Denormalization is ideal for read-heavy applications like data warehousing and reporting systems where performance and query speed are more critical than data integrity.

docs.title: When Normalization is Not Followed
docs.text:
Rules of database normalization are intentionally skipped or broken—a process known as denormalization—when strict table separation hurts system performance or speed.

  • Read-Heavy Workloads:

    When an application reads data much more often than it writes (such as a public-facing catalog or dashboard), joining dozens of normalized tables slows down query response times. Users on Stack Overflow generally agree that denormalizing helps avoid excessive and costly JOIN operations.

  • Data Warehouses and Reporting:

    Analytical systems, business intelligence tools, and OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) cubes store pre-aggregated or redundant data (like star or snowflake schemas with materialized views) to speed up complex historical reporting.

  • High-Performance / Low-Latency Systems:

    When real-time gaming, high-frequency trading, or large-scale web services cannot afford the CPU overhead of stitching together scattered rows across multiple tables, data is duplicated.

  • Prototyping and Early Development:

    During fast iteration, small projects, or simple schemas, rigid normalization adds unnecessary design and coding complexity before performance bottlenecks even exist.

  • Archival and Snapshots:

    Storing historical snapshots (such as freezing a customer's billing address on an old invoice) intentionally breaks normalization so past records do not change if the live user record updates.

docs.title: The Risks of Breaking Normalization
docs.text:
When you bypass normalization, you accept trade-offs that your application code must manage:

  • Data Anomalies:

    Increased risk of update, insertion, and deletion anomalies where duplicate data falls out of sync.

  • Higher Maintenance:

    You often need extra logic, background jobs, or database triggers to keep redundant data consistent.

docs.title: Feature: Authentication — Entity-Relationship Diagram & Build Notes
docs.text: feature/auth is complete: identity, Chairman-issued onboarding, login, roles, and the audit-log foundation every later branch builds on.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Every feature in this system — campaigns, pledges, payments, meetings, reports — depends on one question being answered first: who is doing this, and are they allowed to? feature/auth exists to answer that question properly, once, in a way every later branch can simply rely on rather than re-solving.

This isn't open self-registration. The family already has real, existing governance — a Chairman, a Secretary, a Treasurer — and the system is built to work the way the family actually operates, not to replace it with a generic sign-up form. A member never creates their own account. Membership is issued, deliberately, by someone with the authority to issue it, the same way it would be in a real family meeting: the Chairman says who's in, and the system reflects that decision rather than second-guessing it.

The feature covers five things, each building on the one before it: the family itself as the root of the whole system, the people who belong to it, the roles those people can hold, the credentials that let them prove who they are, and an immutable record of everything that happens along the way. Nothing in this feature is throwaway scaffolding — every table, every constraint, every security decision here is the floor the other twelve feature branches stand on.

docs.title: The Flow — from organization to active member
docs.text:
It starts with the family itself. In this system, a family is the organization — the single tenant the whole platform serves. That root record is established once, holding nothing more than a name and a creation timestamp, and everything else in the database — every member, every campaign, every payment — ultimately traces back to it through a family_id. The schema is built so that supporting more than one family later is possible without a redesign, but v1 deliberately runs with exactly one: this isn't a multi-tenant SaaS product yet, it's one real family's system, built properly from day one.

Once the family exists, someone has to be its first Chairman — the person whose authority everything else flows from. From that point on, onboarding a new member is entirely the Chairman's (or Secretary's) action, not the member's own. The Chairman fills in a new member's basic details — their name, and at least a phone number or an email, so there's somewhere to actually deliver their credentials — and submits it. Nothing about this request mentions which family the new member belongs to; that's deliberately never something the caller gets to choose. It's taken directly from the Chairman's own session, so there's no path by which anyone could onboard a member into a family that isn't theirs.

The moment that request lands, the system generates a temporary password — a short, random string built to avoid characters that look alike on a small phone screen, since this is often read off an SMS by someone who isn't especially comfortable with technology. That password is hashed immediately, the same way any real password would be, and the plain version is never written to the database at all — it exists only long enough to be handed off for delivery, and then it's gone. Alongside it, the system marks this member as needing to change their password before doing anything else, and sets a 48-hour clock on how long that temporary credential is allowed to remain valid.

The new member receives that password — today, as a line printed to a console standing in for a real SMS gateway that doesn't exist yet, but written so that swapping in a real one later changes nothing about how onboarding itself works. They log in with it, and the system checks, in order: does this person actually exist, is their account active, has the 48-hour window already closed, and does the password they typed actually match what was issued. If all of that holds, they're let in — but not all the way in. Because this is still a temporary password, every part of the system except the "change your password" action is closed to them. They can't view a campaign, can't make a payment, can't do anything else, until they've replaced it with something only they know.

Changing it is itself a small, deliberately careful step — the member has to prove they still know the temporary password before they're allowed to replace it, even though they're already holding a valid session token. That's not redundant; it's what stops a stolen token alone from being enough to lock the real member out of their own account. Once the new password is set, the temporary one is gone for good, the forced-change flag clears, and the member is sent back to log in fresh — this time with full access, shaped by whatever roles the Chairman has assigned them.

And every single step along that path — the family's creation, the onboarding, the first login, the password change — leaves a permanent, unchangeable trace: who did it, what changed, and when. Not as an afterthought bolted on at the end, but as part of the same action, inside the same transaction, from the very first branch of this project onward.

docs.title: What's inside feature/auth
docs.text:
• Five database tables

    Family, Member, Role, MemberRole, AuditLog — with foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints enforcing the rules above at the database level, not just trusted to application code.

  • Password security

    bcrypt hashing for every password, temporary or permanent; cryptographically secure random generation for temporary passwords.

  • Session handling

    JWT-based access tokens, signed with a secret kept out of version control.

  • A universal active-account gate

    checked in exactly one place, so a deactivated member is blocked from everything the instant that happens, with no risk of a forgotten endpoint that never learned to check it.

  • Role-based access control

    evaluated as the union of a member's roles, since one person can legitimately hold several at once.

  • A clean separation of layers

    database models, security primitives, business logic, request validation, and HTTP endpoints each live in their own place, so the same logic could be reused outside a web request if it ever needed to be.

  • An audit trail from the first commit

    not retrofitted later, but built in from the very first feature, so every later branch inherits the same discipline automatically.

docs.title: Entity-Relationship Diagram
docs.text:
erDiagram
    FAMILIES ||--o{ MEMBERS : has
    MEMBERS ||--o{ MEMBER_ROLES : holds
    ROLES ||--o{ MEMBER_ROLES : "assigned as"
    FAMILIES ||--o{ AUDIT_LOGS : scopes
    MEMBERS ||--o{ AUDIT_LOGS : "acts in"

    FAMILIES {
        uuid id PK
        string name
        datetime created_at
    }

    MEMBERS {
        uuid id PK
        uuid family_id FK
        string name
        string phone_number UK
        string email UK
        string id_number UK
        boolean is_minor
        boolean is_active
        string hashed_password
        boolean must_change_password
        datetime password_expires_at
        datetime created_at
    }

    ROLES {
        uuid id PK
        string name UK
        string description
    }

    MEMBER_ROLES {
        uuid id PK
        uuid member_id FK
        uuid role_id FK
        datetime assigned_at
    }

    AUDIT_LOGS {
        uuid id PK
        uuid family_id FK
        uuid actor_member_id FK
        string action
        string entity_type
        uuid entity_id
        jsonb before_state
        jsonb after_state
        datetime created_at
    }

Five entities, two deliberate design choices worth highlighting:

  • MEMBER_ROLES is a junction table, not a single role_id column on MEMBERS — because role assignment is many-to-many (a Chairman can also be a contributing Member). A single foreign key can only ever point at one role; the junction table is what lets a member hold several roles at once.
  • Minors are MEMBERS rows too, not a separate table — is_minor is a flag, with phone_number/email/hashed_password left NULL. This keeps every other relationship that points at a member (future Pledge, Payment, Attendance tables) working unchanged for minors, with no parallel structures needed.

docs.title: How it was built — layered, bottom to top
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["models/ — SQLAlchemy ORM<br/>5 tables, constraints, relationships"] --> B["Alembic migration<br/>generated & applied to Postgres"]
    B --> C["core/ — security, exceptions, permissions<br/>password hashing · JWT · RBAC"]
    C --> D["services/ — business logic<br/>audit_service · auth_service"]
    D --> E["schemas/ — Pydantic validation<br/>request/response contracts"]
    E --> F["routers/ — HTTP endpoints<br/>/auth/onboard · /auth/login · /auth/change-password"]

Each layer only depends on the one below it — routers knows about schemas and services, but services never imports FastAPI at all. That separation is what lets the same auth_service.onboard_member() function be called from a web request today, and from a CLI script or background job later, with zero changes.

docs.title: The onboarding → login → forced change flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Chairman
    participant R as Router
    participant S as auth_service
    participant DB as Postgres

    C->>R: POST /auth/onboard
    R->>S: onboard_member()
    S->>S: generate temp password, hash it
    S->>DB: INSERT member (must_change_password=true)
    S-->>C: temp password "sent" via SMS stub

    Note over C: Member logs in with temp password

    C->>R: POST /auth/login
    R->>S: authenticate()
    S->>DB: verify is_active, password hash, expiry
    S-->>C: access token (must_change_password=true)

    Note over C: Restricted to change-password only

    C->>R: POST /auth/change-password
    R->>S: change_password()
    S->>DB: UPDATE hashed_password, clear flags
    S-->>C: success — must log in again

docs.title: Security measures built into this feature
docs.text:
• Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, never stored in plain text — not even the temporary one.
  • JWT-based sessions, signed with a secret key kept out of version control (.env, gitignored).
  • is_active is checked in exactly one place — the point a token resolves back to a member — so a deactivated member is blocked from everything the instant Chairman flips the switch.
  • Role-based access control evaluates the union of a member's roles, not a single assumed role, since one person can hold several.
  • Database-level CHECK constraints back up application-level validation — e.g. an adult member must have a phone or email, enforced by Postgres itself, not just trusted to the API layer.
  • Every onboarding, login, and password change writes an immutable audit log entry — actor, action, before/after state, timestamp.

docs.title: What's deliberately deferred
docs.text: • Real SMS delivery — send_sms() is a stub that logs to console; swapping in a gateway later requires no change to the code.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization with FastAPI
docs.text:
• Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of the user, while authorization determines whether the authenticated user has the right to perform certain actions. In the FastAPI, these concepts can be implemented using dependencies and middleware of the application.

  • FastAPI supports multiple flexible authentication methods natively through its fastapi.security module. Because it integrates seamlessly with FastAPI's dependency injection system (Depends), protecting your routes automatically documents the security schemes inside your interactive /docs (Swagger UI).

Note

The best and most standard authentication method to use in FastAPI for user-facing applications is OAuth2 with Password Flow and JSON Web Tokens (JWT)

docs.title: Why You Should Use JWT with OAuth2 Bearer Tokens
docs.text:
• Stateless: The server does not need to store session data in a database or memory for every single request. The token holds the user identity.
  • Built-in Support: FastAPI provides native utilities like OAuth2PasswordBearer in fastapi.security that integrate directly with the interactive Swagger UI documentation.
  • Scalable: It works exceptionally well for modern single-page applications (SPAs), mobile apps, and microservices.

docs.title: Alternative Authentication Methods Based on Your Use Case
docs.text:
1. API Keys (Custom Headers, Queries, or Cookies)
    • API Key authentication maps a unique, long-lived string to a specific consumer. FastAPI allows you to look for these keys in three locations: standard request headers, query parameters, or cookies.
    • Best For: Public-facing developer APIs, third-party integrations, and machine-to-machine scripts. FastAPI Tools Used: APIKeyHeader, APIKeyQuery, APIKeyCookie.

  2. HTTP Basic Authentication

    • HTTP Basic Auth sends the raw username and password encoded in Base64 within the Authorization: Basic header with every single request.

    • Best For: Internal APIs, administrative scripts, cron jobs, and quick prototypes.

      • Warning

      Warning: Base64 is only an encoding, not encryption. This must only be served over HTTPS / TLS.

      • FastAPI Tools Used: HTTPBasic, HTTPBasicCredentials.

    • Session-Based Authentication:

      • Instead of sending a token or credential with every request, the server tracks active user states via a signed session cookie.

      • FastAPI Tools Used: Unlike OAuth2 or Basic Auth, FastAPI doesn't provide a rigid built-in UI helper for sessions, but it relies on underlying starlette.middleware.sessions.SessionMiddleware or third-party libraries like fastapi-users.

      • Best For: Server-rendered frontend applications where instant logout capability is vital (state can be revoked on the server instantly).Also Best if you are building traditional server-rendered web pages where immediate server-side logout capability is mandatory

docs.title: JWT /OAuth2 (Framework) Authentication Methods
docs.text:
!!! note 
    This is my prefered authentication method for this project

We use two industry standards that work hand-in-hand to secure your API:

  1. OAuth2 (Framework):
    • It's a protocol that defines how a user logs in. In this project, we use the Password Flow. It handles the "handshake" receiving the username/password and defining how the security "lock" appears in your FastAPI Swagger docs.
  2. JWT (Token):
    • It is the actual "key card" issued after a successful OAuth2 login. It is a compact, signed string containing the user's identity. Because it is cryptographically signed, the server can trust it in subsequent requests without re-checking the password every time.

docs.title: Why JWT Is the Best Fit for FastAPI
docs.text:
1. Stateless by design :
    • a JWT carries its own claims (user id, roles, expiry) and is verified using a signature check, not a database/session lookup. This matches FastAPI's async, horizontally-scalable nature — any instance of your app can verify a token without shared state.
  2. First-class framework support :
    • OAuth2PasswordBearer combined with python-jose/PyJWT is the pattern used in FastAPI's own official documentation, meaning strong community support, tooling, and fewer surprises.
  3. Frontend-agnostic :
    • the same token format works whether the client is a React SPA, a mobile app, or another backend service calling yours. Self-contained authorization :
    • roles/permissions can be embedded directly as claims, reducing the need for a database round-trip on every request just to check "what can this user do?"
  4. Solves its own weaknesses with two additions:
    • Short-lived access tokens : limit the damage window if a token is ever leaked.
    • Longer-lived refresh tokens : let the user stay logged in without repeatedly re-entering credentials, while giving you a controlled point to revoke access.

docs.title: The Procedure JWT Authentication Follows:
docs.text:
1. Registration
    • user submits credentials; password is hashed (bcrypt/argon2) and stored — never in plain text.
  2. Login
    • user submits credentials again; server verifies the password against the stored hash.
  3. Token issuance
    • on success, the server issues a short-lived access token (5–15 min), and a longer-lived refresh token (days/weeks) both cryptographically signed with a secret key.
  4. Token delivery
    • tokens are set as httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, so client-side JavaScript cannot read them (blocks XSS token theft), while the browser still auto-attaches them to requests.
  5. Authenticated requests
    • every protected endpoint call automatically includes the access token cookie.
  6. Verification
    • a FastAPI dependency intercepts the request, checks the token's signature and expiry, and extracts the user's identity/claims before allowing the request through.
  7. Silent refresh
    • once the access token expires, the client calls a /refresh endpoint with the refresh token; if valid (and not blocklisted), a new access token is issued transparently.
  8. Logout / revocation
    • clears both cookies and, ideally, adds the refresh token's ID to a revocation list so it cannot be reused even before its natural expiry.

docs.title: How This Achieves High Security in FastAPI
docs.text:
1. Password hashing (bcrypt/argon2)
    • plaintext passwords never touch the database or logs, so even a DB breach doesn't expose credentials directly.
  2. Signed tokens
    • any tampering with the payload invalidates the signature, so a stolen/modified token is instantly rejected on verification.
  3. httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies
    • removes the two classic JWT weak points:
      • XSS — JavaScript can't read an httpOnly cookie, so injected scripts can't steal the token.
      • CSRF — SameSite=strict (or double-submit tokens) stops other sites from silently riding on the cookie.
  4. Short access token lifetime
    • shrinks the exploitation window if a token does leak; it's naturally useless within minutes.
  5. jti (token ID) blocklist in Redis
    • checked on the refresh flow (not every request, to preserve performance) so a specific compromised refresh token can be revoked immediately.
  6. token_version / token_valid_after field on the user record
    • a coarser "log out everywhere" switch. Bumping this instantly invalidates every token issued before that moment — useful for suspected full account compromise.
  7. Dependency injection for verification
    • FastAPI's Depends() pattern centralizes token verification logic in one place, reducing the chance of a route accidentally skipping the auth check.

docs.title: When implementing JWT authentication in FastAPI, use these modern libraries:
docs.text:
• PyJWT: For generating and verifying signed JWTs.
  • pwdlib (with argon2): For secure password hashing instead of older libraries like passlib.
  • pydantic-settings: For securely loading environment variables and secret keys.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• FastAPI gives you three practical authentication schemes, and choosing between them is a question about your clients rather than about the framework.

  • Basic auth is the simplest and the most limited. Use it over HTTPS for internal APIs and nothing else. API keys identify machine clients well and revoke cleanly, which makes them the right default for public APIs. Sessions fit browser applications and are the only one of the three where logging out genuinely ends access.

Note

Whichever you pick, the practices underneath do not change: hash every stored credential, load secrets from the environment, rate limit the login endpoint, compare secrets in constant time, and serve everything over TLS. Those five apply to token-based authentication too, and they are what separates a working authentication system from a secure one.

docs.title: User Research Analysis
docs.text:
Info

This is the FAMILY CONTRIBUTION MANAGEMENT SYSTEM whereby the vision is to digitize how families manage meetings, contributions, campaigns, events, and payments

Before any feature was designed, research was conducted with family members across different age groups — young and old — to understand how the family currently manages contributions, what's frustrating about it, and what a better system would actually need to do for them.

Note

"Methodology" Research was conducted through one-on-one interviews. Questions were posed directly to each interviewee, and their responses were recorded for analysis.

docs.title: Research Questions
docs.text:
Before any schema or endpoint was designed, this started with talking to the people who would actually use it — the section below captures the questions that shaped everything that follows below.

Tip

"Questions were tailored by age and tech familiarity" The same underlying topics were explored with every interviewee, but phrasing and follow-up depth varied by age and tech comfort — younger family members generally have far more exposure to technology than older members, whose tech familiarity is often minimal. Adjusting how each question was asked (without changing what it was really asking) made sure older, less tech-familiar members could answer just as fully as younger ones.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1.How would you describe the perfect family management system, in your own words?

2.Which feature would you most want included in the system, and how would that feature help with something that's currently hard to do?

3.What challenges has the manual way of handling things caused for you, and what do you expect a system to solve?

4.What does "modernizing" the family's record-keeping and payments with technology mean to you, and how do you think it would improve the way family records and payments are handled?

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: The following was the feedback recorded after the questions were asked . I interviewed different family members and recorded their answers based on different questions asked.

docs.title: Challenges during the interview process
docs.text:
• Some family members epecially the (old members) had difficulties understanding the tech related questions but I had to take extra time to explain some of the questions to them.

tip

Despite some members having challenges answering some questions , The interview process was seamles and it gave me great insight to build the system to solve the challenges the members are facing.

docs.title: Feature requests & convenience
docs.text:
A younger member (20s, tech-comfortable) felt the payment process should be automated so that they can pay from the comfort of their own phone, rather than needing to hand over cash or make a manual transfer and then separately report it. They also wanted the system to automatically update their payment record and send a receipt confirming the payment went through, so they're not left wondering whether it registered.

Quote

"The family system should ease my payment process by either prompting me to make the payment."

— Younger member, 20s, tech-comfortable

docs.title: Reducing manual calculation errors
docs.text:
A Treasurer-adjacent member in their 60s felt the system should make payment records automatic and handle the money calculations itself, rather than leaving that to memory. Tracking payments manually — adding up who's paid, who hasn't, what's left — was tiring to keep up with, and compiling the records by hand left room for mistakes.

Quote

"The system should help with the money calculations."

— Treasurer-adjacent member, 60s

docs.title: Automated reporting & reducing paperwork
docs.text: The Secretary said the system should produce the annual report in time for the December AGM meeting on its own — compiling all the year's records by hand takes time, and by the end of that process it's easy to get tired and leave some details out. They wanted the system to surface feedback/summaries on every campaign as it closes, not just once a year, and to generate the full annual report automatically. They also pointed out that members should be able to download meeting minutes straight to their phone, removing the need to print and distribute hardcopy minutes, which is a real, recurring cost.

docs.title: Reminders & notifications
docs.text:
A member in their 30s said the system should send them reminders — for upcoming events, meetings, and any campaign that needs money — because work keeps their mind busy and it's easy to lose track of family matters in the meantime. For them, reminders aren't a nice-to-have; they're what keeps them able to stay involved in family events at all.

Quote

"I want to receive reminders and notification on my phone of any upcoming event or function."

— Member, 30s

docs.title: Insight
docs.text:
Success

The system's real job, based on this research, isn't just digitizing records — it's removing the family's collective reliance on individual memory.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Talking to these four family members — a young professional who just wants paying his dues to be as easy as tapping his phone, an older Treasurer-adjacent relative tired of doing money math in his head, a Secretary who dreads the December scramble to compile a year's worth of records before the AGM, and a busy 30-something who's genuinely afraid of missing family events because work crowds everything else out — made one thing clear: this was never really a request for an "app." It was a request to be relieved of a mental load that's been quietly falling on whoever happens to be paying attention, or holding the role, at any given moment.

What stood out most was how consistent the underlying need was, even though the four people asking for it couldn't be more different in age, role, and comfort with technology. Nobody asked for something flashy.

Example

Every feature built from here on should be traceable back to a real thing a real family member said, not just to what seemed technically interesting to build.

They asked for reminders that actually reach them, numbers they don't have to double-check by hand, reports that write themselves instead of being assembled under deadline pressure, and confirmation that a payment really went through. Small, specific, entirely reasonable asks — and together, they form a pretty complete blueprint for what "done well" looks like for this system.
